articles.title_orig: Banks Preparing for Aftermath of Unprecedented Catastrophe Caused by AI
articles.title_zh: Banks Preparing for Aftermath of Unprecedented Catastrophe Caused by AI
articles.content_orig:
Doomsaying about the coming AI apocalypse is no longer relegated to outbursts from a few tech billionaires .
Now, the major American banks whose policies dictate the flow of capital throughout the world are starting to worry about rogue AI, preparing contingency plans for the “day after” a theoretical AI-driven catastrophe.
That’s according to new reporting from Axios , which notes that banks are preparing for the worst as they experience a huge rise in AI agent activity on behalf of individual customers.
The main worry seems to be an influx of financial activity driven by autonomous AI agents, which have been authorized to access bank accounts by their human users. In some cases, as Axios noted previously , those agents are making moves that haven’t explicitly been prompted by humans — a few even going so far as to contact call centers on behalf of their users, without being instructed to do so.
That’s become a major liability for top banks like Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo, which are scrambling to implement security procedures and policy updates to get ahead of the AI swarm.
Failing to stay on top of emerging risks, some experts say, could result in financial catastrophe. As chief economist at the Apollo wealth management firm Torsten Slok explained in a late September brief , AI agents operating under instructions to “optimize the return” on their users’ money could mean banks “lose a large share of the cheap deposits they rely on to make loans, which would be a problem for the entire financial system.”
As skeevy as that admission is, there’s plenty of truth in the fact that our for-profit banking system is simply not designed to handle that volume of consumer-friendly optimization. A casino whose slot machines paid out to every player wouldn’t stay in business very long, after all.
Other finance gurus have pointed to the fact that AI agents might simply go haywire, regardless of what they’ve been instructed to do.
“You’re assuming they’re going to act properly on your behalf and they may not,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon told a room full of economists and financial experts in Chicago earlier this month. “You can’t stop it. You just have to, like, manage the hell out of it.”

articles.title_zh: China urges US to halt proposed expansion of outbound investment curbs
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Treasury Department is moving to restrict American investment in China’s life sciences industry, releasing long-anticipated proposed rules that add biotechnology to the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act.
Published Thursday, the draft regulations (PDF) categorize “pharmaceutical compounds” as a “prohibited technology” that would trigger an outright ban on certain outbound transactions with “countries of concern,” such as China. The definition of pharmaceutical compounds runs the gamut of different modalities, spanning small molecules, polymers, vaccines, blood products, allergenics, cell and gene therapies, monoclonal antibodies and other recombinant therapeutic proteins, as well as their delivery systems.
If implemented in its current form, the rules would cause additional headaches for U.S. biopharmas looking to tap into China’s biotech innovations. But despite the sweeping scope of the ban covering various types of drug molecules, biopharma business development teams can breathe a measured sigh of relief.
The proposed rule largely spares the regular in-licensing deals and fee-for-service drug R&D collaborations that have driven the majority of multi-billion-dollar deals between Western biopharma companies and their Chinese counterparts. This detail fits the description of a Reuters report in September, which said the Treasury was working on rules that would continue to allow pharma companies to strike most licensing deals for Chinese drugs.
In an accompanying Q&A (PDF), the Treasury Department outlined the types of investment that would be covered under its rules: “Under the proposed rule, certain transactions that involve the acquisition of equity, provision of debt financing that is convertible to equity or that carries certain rights, greenfield investments or other corporate expansions, the creation of joint ventures, or certain LP investments would be covered.
“Activities that do not meet the definition of a covered national security transaction would not be subject to the program except where they are undertaken to evade or avoid the proposed rule,” the agency explained.
Therefore, traditional asset licensing agreements, where Western drugmakers pay cash, milestones and sales royalties for ex-China rights to drugs, fall outside the scope of covered transactions.
The language of the rules matches the current text of the COINS Act itself. COINS was enacted as part of the fiscal year 2026 national defense bill, giving the Treasury the power to scrutinize—or outright prohibit—American investments in sensitive foreign sectors involving countries it views as adversaries. While the law does not name biotech, it allows Treasury to add new sectors when devising specific rules.
When calls for including biotechnology in the COINS Act emerged earlier this year, Laurie Burlingame, a lawyer at Morse, Barnes-Brown & Pendleton, who specializes in life sciences transactions, explained to Fierce that a pure sectoral expansion of the law likely wouldn’t cover pharma licensing deals, as the law is highly focused on equity investments rather than usual product transactions.
Several high-profile U.S. Big Pharma deals with Chinese companies have drawn scrutiny from Washington’s China hawks in their COINS Act expansion push. But those transactions appear to be pure licensing agreements based on public announcements. These include Bristol Myers Squibb’s potential $15.2 billion deal with Hengrui Pharma covering 13 early-stage programs.
However, some other transaction types that have gained traction lately would fall victim to the rules.
The COINS Act lists “acquisition of an equity interest” in a Chinese entity as a “covered national security transaction.” This provision would prevent U.S. venture capital firms from investing in Chinese biotechs, and it would also impact future deals resembling Pfizer’s recent partnership with 3SBio.
When Pfizer in-licensed a PD-1xVEGF bispecific antibody from 3SBio last year, the New York pharma made a $100 million equity investment in the Chinese biotech. That deal structure would be prohibited under the proposed Treasury rules.
Burlingame previously raised concerns over the COINS Act’s potential impact on the “NewCo” model, in which venture capitalists form a new U.S. biotech based on assets licensed from China. The Chinese licensor often takes an equity stake in the new firm to capture long-term upside.
Under existing COINS language, only Chinese ownership of 50% or above would make the NewCo a target as a Chinese entity. But the proposed Treasury rules’ anti-evasion clause could subject any future China deals that involve an equity interest component to additional scrutiny.
In addition, “entrance into a joint venture” also marks a notable transaction category regulated by the COINS Act.
In its proposed rules, the Treasury deliberately chose not to define “joint venture,” instead, it “refers to the plain English meaning of the term, i.e., as involving the contribution of capital and/or assets by two parties and the sharing of profits and losses.”
This murky definition adds uncertainties to some deals. In Pfizer’s $10.5 billion , 12-asset collaboration with Innovent Biologics, the two companies will co-develop four programs globally and share the development costs, plus U.S. and European profits or losses. Although this unincorporated partnership doesn’t necessarily fit the common idea of a joint venture business, it does involve the contribution of capital from both parties to fund R&D and profit-sharing, and the Treasury said that its term “would not require the establishment or formation of a new entity.”
It’s not immediately clear if the Treasury means to crack down on this deal structure. If it does, the Pfizer-Innovent accord could face regulatory actions—only transactions completed before the enactment of the COINS Act on Dec. 18, 2025, are exempt from the Treasury rules, if implemented.
Following the release of the draft rules, the biopharma industry has reacted with a cautious tone, warning against any broadly restrictive provisions as they study the policy’s details.
“The Administration is correct that biotechnology is a strategic technology industry for the United States. We need policies and initiatives that maintain and advance our global leadership in biotech, particularly as we compete with China,” John Crowley, president and CEO of the influential biotech industry lobby group Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO), said in a statement Thursday.
“The details of the proposed Treasury Department rules matter. We cannot restrict our way to success,” he continued. “As Treasury considers comments on the proposed rule, we need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors and that may unintentionally risk weakening U.S. biotech competitiveness.”
In a separate statement, Kendalle Burlin O’Connell, CEO and president of Massachusetts biotech trade association MassBio, said that “efforts to address national security risks must be carefully targeted to avoid undermining the innovation ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader in developing new medicines.”
“For Massachusetts’ biotech industry, international partnerships and licensing agreements can bring promising scientific discoveries into the U.S. drug development pipeline, where American companies invest in and advance potential new therapies,” she added. “Preserving the ability to develop breakthrough innovations from our own world-leading domestic pipeline while also identifying promising innovations from elsewhere is essential to maintaining America's competitive advantage and access for U.S. patients.”
The Treasury Department is seeking comments until Dec. 7, 2026. Apparently recognizing the risk of collateral damage to public health and legitimate business conduct, the agency is explicitly asking for feedback on “whether and how ‘pharmaceutic

articles.title_orig: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.title_zh: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.
Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.
Meghan said in a statement Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and that she was previously informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.
A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said a review of records confirmed that the force received a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”
“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex,” the statement added. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”
The statement did not say whether any investigation took place or if any further action was taken.
The force said it was reviewing the incident and considering whether to refer itself to the United Kingdom’s Independent Office for Police Conduct.
Asked about the discrepancy between the two statements on the date of the letter, a spokesperson for Meghan told NBC News she “may have been mistaken by a few months.”
The allegations against Thomas Markle were first reported Thursday by The Sun, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home.
The Sun published a photo it said showed the son, Thomas Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated.
“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, whose relationship with her father has been limited and fraught in recent years. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.
She said the letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018 “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
Meghan added that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
His daughter Samantha Markle also dismissed her brother’s allegations, telling the Daily Mail that “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever. ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.
In a statement, the FBI said it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.
The couple last week made their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K. , visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: U.K. police say they received letter with claims against Meghan's father, wasn't shared with other law enforcement
articles.title_zh: U.K. police say they received letter with claims against Meghan's father, wasn't shared with other law enforcement
articles.content_orig:
A letter making a "number of claims" against the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, a Scotland Yard spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Saturday.
Police said they passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess "for their awareness," however, the details of the allegations made in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
On Friday, it was reported that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement Saturday that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
"At this point, investigators are looking into the nature and origin of the materials and whether these may be connected to any violation of law," Col. Allen Rae Co said in a statement. "U.S. authorities have also offered assistance should Philippine authorities determine that their support is needed as the investigation progresses."
The British tabloid The Sun was the first to report the allegations against Markle Sr. The report said the younger Markle allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.
Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News on Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports about her father. She said she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.
Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.
Responding to Saturday's developments dating the letter to 2019, a spokesman for the duchess told CBS News partner BBC News that "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time."
Scotland Yard said Saturday that Met Police will be reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and deciding whether to refer itself to the police watchdog.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: U.S. intel memo warns of "advanced" Iranian plots to kill officials abroad
articles.title_zh: Scoop: U.S. intel memo warns of "advanced" Iranian plots to kill officials abroad
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title_orig: Holiday flights from Portland are getting pricier. Should you book now?
articles.title_zh: Holiday flights from Portland are getting pricier. Should you book now?
articles.content_orig:
A worker fuels a United Airlines plane at Salt Lake City International Airport in April, 2026. The price of jet fuel, one of airlines' biggest expenses, is close to an all-time high in the U.S. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption
BALTIMORE — Herb and Latasha Williams flew from Dallas to Baltimore/Washington International Airport this week for a quick vacation to celebrate his birthday.
But their plane tickets cost hundreds of dollars more than they expected. And Latasha Williams is now wondering if they can afford to travel for the holidays.
"I kind of wanted to go somewhere warm. Florida, I'm thinking," she said.
Then she looked at airfares.
"Maybe next year. Maybe," she said with a laugh. "Fingers crossed."
Those planning to fly this holiday season, should be prepared to pay more than they did last year. Experts expect airfares for this holiday travel season will be the highest in years as airlines scramble to cover the rising cost of jet fuel, which is one of their biggest expenses.
The average price of jet fuel in the U.S. reached $4.90 per gallon on Thursday, according to the tracking firm Argus. That's the highest single-day average the firm has ever recorded, and more than twice what the price was a year ago.
"Airfares right now are at what we see as a 10-year high because of the high cost of jet fuel," said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper, a travel tech company. "Airlines have to pass on these super high jet fuel prices in the form of higher fares to consumers."
Airfares for Thanksgiving are up about 30% compared to last year, according to Berg. Tickets for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20%.
But so far, Berg said, travelers seem willing to pay, at least for their big holiday trips.
"We're at the time of year where travel is really sticky. Even with higher prices, travelers are unlikely to make major changes to their traditional holiday home for the holiday trips," Berg said in an interview with NPR.
U.S. airlines say demand is holding steady even as fares have gone up. In an earnings call this month, Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said consumers have put up a "limited amount of resistance" and still view airfare as "reasonably affordable" even after fare increases.
"I think that's a very good sign for the future," Bastian said.
Some in the industry think fares will go even higher next year.
"You could see airfares rise next year in Europe. I think by 10, 15, maybe 20 percent," Michael O'Leary, CEO of the European low-cost carrier Ryanair, said this week in Belgium. "You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months."
The picture may be slightly better in the U.S., which has more oil-producing and refining capacity than Europe. Still, higher fuel costs are hurting U.S. carriers, too.
"The airlines themselves are eating most of that cost,"  Chris Sununu, the head of Airlines for America, a trade group representing the big airlines, said in an interview this week with CNBC. "And some of it unfortunately has to be passed on to the customer and so you see that 20 to 30 percent increase as we go into the holidays."
Consumers are shopping around more in search of better deals, Berg said, and booking their tickets earlier to try to lock in reasonable prices.
"Usually I am shouting from the rooftops in the middle of October, 'Book your holiday travel by the end of this month, prices will not go down from here,'" Berg said. "But we actually saw an increase in customers booking holiday travel in September already."
At the airport in Baltimore, some travelers say they're priced out of flying for the holidays this year altogether.
"I'm gonna have to drive," said Rachel Stern of Frederick, Maryland. "I'm from Chicago originally, so I'm gonna drive. For me and my kids, just too much to get tickets."
But others said they're resigned to paying more for their holiday tickets. Mary Haller of Bethany Beach, Delaware is planning a trip to Europe.
"Literally I looked at the economy tickets two weeks ago and they have gone up," Haler said. "It was significant and I sort of had shell shock."
Still, Haller said she has little choice but to buy the tickets anyway.
"I feel bad for people who don't have the means to pay the extra money," she said.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.title_zh: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.content_orig:
United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran is in “advanced stages” of plans to target US personnel abroad, prompting Washington to place staff on high alert in the Middle East, according to US officials and an official memo cited by Axios and The New York Times (NYT).
The alert comes as the US and Israel signal they may be preparing for a new military campaign against Iran, which Tehran has reportedly threatened to retaliate against, in part by targeting communications cables in the Gulf.
The heightened threat assessment has prompted Washington, already on guard over escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, to trim Washington’s diplomatic presence in the Middle East, the NYT has reported, citing officials.
Here’s what we know about the latest US warning, and how it fits into the broader US-Iran conflict:
A warning about Iranian plans to target US citizens was detailed in a memo sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, first reported by US news site Axios.
In the memo, Clayton wrote that US agencies had received intelligence indicating that Iran has “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” overseas, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries.
The NYT, which also reported on the memo, cited unnamed US officials as saying threats to American officials, including ambassadors, had been assessed in recent weeks, and that Iran had lined up potential targets in Europe.
The officials said some intelligence indicates Iranian operatives are already active within the US.
Washington has not publicly commented on the memo, although the NYT cited a US official as confirming its authenticity on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration.
Another official cited by the NYT played down Iran’s ability to execute attacks inside the US and elsewhere, saying it lacks the capacity to follow through on all its ambitions.
According to officials cited by the NYT, US agencies deem Iranian threats to US citizens in the Middle East to be “at the highest level” since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
This assessment is behind the US’s recent moves to withdraw staff posted in the region, the NYT added.
In the background are reported US and Israel plans to initiate a new military campaign against Iran following the US mid-term elections next month . On Friday, Trump said the US “may do another little epic fury”, using the codename for the US-Israel war against Iran that began on February 28.
On Wednesday, the US Department of State announced it was removing non-essential staff in its embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi infrastructure.
Staff levels have also been quietly reduced at other US diplomatic missions in the region, several US media have reported. That includes embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Lebanon, according to CNN.
A US official cited by the NYT said the threat of Houthi attacks and “Iranian terror plots targeting US officials” were driving US staffing decisions.
Iran has not responded to news of the US intelligence memo accusing it of planning attacks on US personnel.
However, Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened and carried out attacks against US bases and those of its allies in the region. The Pentagon has confirmed that 21 US military personnel have been killed in the Middle East since the war on Iran began.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that Tehran would follow a new “offensive” strategy if the US renewed attacks.
That means Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes, said IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, adding that the quality, range and power of Iranian missiles had improved.
Tehran also has in-depth plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of new US-Israeli attacks, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two senior Iranian security officials.
Previously, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities across the region could come under attack if war with the US breaks out again.
Yes, US authorities have long accused Iran of being behind plots targeting US citizens, including assassination attempts against Trump on US soil.
In March this year, a Pakistani national was convicted by a US court of plotting to assassinate Trump and other US politicians on the orders of Iran’s IRGC.
An Iranian IRGC member was charged in 2022 with trying to assassinate former US National Security Advisor John Bolton. The individual allegedly “attempted to pay individuals in the United States $300,000 to carry out the murder in Washington DC or Maryland”, according to the US Department of Justice.
Last year, the US intelligence community warned that Iran would “continue to directly threaten US persons globally”, specifically targeting officials it believed were involved in the 2020 assassination of IRGC Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani .
This month, the US abruptly withdrew bombers from an airbase in England, United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. That followed a security incident at the base, after which the UK arrested several men on suspicion of working with Iranian intelligence.

articles.title_orig: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay
articles.title_zh: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay
articles.content_orig:
Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing , airline executives say that's just fine.
At the New York Hilton in Midtown Manhattan on Friday night, the aviation industry held its annual Wings Club gala, honoring Ed Bastian, CEO of profit-leader Delta Air Lines .
North American airline CEOs and other executives at the black-tie bash told CNBC that demand trends aren't worrying them, but persistently high, profit-crimping fuel prices are.
The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares matters more than fully filling planes or flying record numbers of travelers.
"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Plane ticket prices have skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.
Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.
The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's revenue passenger count, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.
"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.
Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints than in the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. That's down less than 2% from last year, but it follows years of growth.
With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices at $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that overall travel demand is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.
And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than a year ago and said its unit revenue rose 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.
"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Most airlines expect fuel costs to keep biting, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 per gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from $3.90 per gallon in the third.
American, United, Delta and Southwest all cut their 2026 profit forecasts this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.
American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back its capacity expansion goals, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.
"Today, we find ourselves yet at another inflection point for our industry and the world. ... Geopolitics affecting our business, driving the price of jet fuel to historic highs," Bastian said in his award-acceptance speech, adding that artificial intelligence makes it hard to predict months or weeks ahead.
"It causes many people to question yet again the durability of our industry. But I'm not worried because I know the people in this room, and I know your resilience and how you've demonstrated that time and time again," he said.
Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, starting with JetBlue Airways next week, followed by Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air , have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.
Many of the problems that plagued the airline industry for years are starting to abate.
In some cases, aircraft deliveries are still years behind schedule. But Boeing , whose CEO, Kelly Ortberg, attended on Friday night, and its main rival, Airbus, have ramped up production. Boeing will update investors on its production outlook when it reports quarterly results Tuesday.
The Federal Aviation Administration has approved Boeing's Max 7, a key smaller jet for Southwest Airlines, and the Max 10, which Alaska Airlines and United Airlines have been waiting for for years.
Pratt & Whitney parent, RTX , and GE Aerospace say they're improving engine durability and shop visit turnaround time, though customers say more improvements are needed.

articles.title_orig: 'It's not something that gets done overnight': SpaceX's telecom ambitions will be hard-won, CEOs and analysts say
articles.title_zh: 'It's not something that gets done overnight': SpaceX's telecom ambitions will be hard-won, CEOs and analysts say
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Elon Musk wants SpaceX ( SPCX ) to take on America's largest cell service providers, but matching the telecom giants' vast wireless networks could take years and billions of dollars, executives and analysts warned this week.
SpaceX, which already operates the world's largest commercial satellite network with Starlink, is in talks with major telecommunications infrastructure companies to secure access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States, Bloomberg reported. The move would advance Musk's ambitions to establish a fourth nationwide wireless carrier alongside the three traditional telecom and mobile service incumbents: Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T ( T ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ).
The announcement sent stock in AT&T and T-Mobile falling by as much as 6% on Friday, while Verizon declined by a thinner 1.5%.
Satellite launches through Starlink and spectrum acquisitions "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call.
But breaking into an industry whose dominant players have spent decades building out infrastructure, acquiring spectrum, and cultivating millions of subscribers will be no easy feat.
"It's not something that gets done overnight," AT&T CEO John Stankey told analysts on his company's earnings call Wednesday, before the latest details of SpaceX's plans emerged. "It takes a lot of years and a huge level of investment to get to the kind of performance levels that customers have become accustomed to in scaled networks."
SpaceX's tower negotiations, which reportedly include cell tower operator Crown Castle ( CCI ), represent one of the clearest indications yet of the scale of SpaceX's ambitions. They also illustrate the substantial financial and technological barriers facing Musk as he attempts to challenge America's entrenched telecommunications giants.
The company's reported target of 80,000 cell sites would put its planned network on a scale comparable to that of the three incumbents. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile each lease space on approximately 60,000 to 80,000 US cell towers combined, according to Goldman Sachs analysts, while the country has roughly 175,000 traditional cell towers nationwide, per data from SNL Kagan.
The cost for such a build-out would be immense, even for a company with the capitalization and balance sheet of SpaceX. The average cellular tenant pays roughly $50,000 per year to lease space on a cell tower, according to Goldman Sachs analysts led by Michael Ng. At that rate, an 80,000-tower network could generate approximately $4 billion in annual rental payments, or between $20 billion and $40 billion over a typical five- to 10-year leasing period.
That estimate also assumes all 80,000 proposed sites are traditional towers, and it leaves out costs for equipment, backhaul infrastructure, operations, and other investments needed to construct and operate a competitive wireless network.
Even so, the scale of the expense underscores the enormous barriers to entry. Though Musk's ambitions for mobile coverage have been held up as a major challenge for the three telecom incumbents, industry leaders and analysts see any potential threat coming further down the road.
"Tower lease agreements to support this deployment [are] the next catalyst," Goldman's analysts wrote to clients. "Although this is not a lease agreement, this is progression toward that catalyst."
SpaceX recently made its first real incursion into the space in early October with the reported $8 billion purchase of a nationwide portfolio of low-band spectrum wireless licenses. Low-band frequencies can travel longer distances and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency spectrum, making them particularly valuable for widespread wireless coverage.
Under the terms of the deal, which remains subject to FCC regulation, Musk's company has agreed to acquire up to 14 megahertz of paired low-band spectrum in the 800 MHz range. AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, by contrast, already hold extensive low-band spectrum portfolios, giving them an established advantage in providing nationwide coverage. Looking for its own advantage, SpaceX plans to combine its newly acquired spectrum with ground-based antennas and cell towers alongside Starlink satellites, creating a hybrid terrestrial and satellite network.
AT&T alone operates between six and eight low-band spectrum carriers in metropolitan markets, Stankey said on Wednesday — a network that also includes antenna systems installed inside hospitals, high-rises, stadiums, and other buildings, an important distinction for dense metropolitan areas. While SpaceX may represent competition for companies like AT&T, UBS analyst John Hodulik recently wrote to clients that specter is likely to be a ways off.
"A Starlink wireless network build remains an overhang [for AT&T], but we believe the multiple will appear increasingly challenging as growth accelerates over the next 12 months and it takes time for Starlink to scale its ambitions," Hodulik wrote.
All that said, SpaceX's ambitions arrive as the traditional boundaries of the telecommunications industry are beginning to blur. Cable providers like Comcast, for example, have aggressively expanded into the wireless market without building their own nationwide cellular networks. The company recently added 368,000 wireless lines in the third quarter, bringing its total to approximately 10.6 million, even as its core broadband business lost 144,000 subscribers.
Rather than funding the kind of infrastructure operated by AT&T and Verizon, Comcast relies on wholesale agreements with existing wireless carriers and its extensive residential Wi-Fi network. Approximately 90% of Xfinity Mobile traffic travels over Wi-Fi, Comcast executives said on the company's earnings call Thursday, allowing Comcast to avoid much of the expense associated with traditional cellular operations.
Comcast's less traditional model raises the possibility that SpaceX could become more than simply another competitor fighting to win existing mobile subscribers, as Comcast already partners with Starlink to provide satellite connectivity to enterprise customers, executives told analysts earlier in the week.
The combination of SpaceX's existing satellite capacity with terrestrial infrastructure could eventually allow the company to serve customers and applications that fall outside the economics of existing wireless networks — even if matching the performance of AT&T or Verizon in major cities proves considerably more challenging.
For the three big telecoms, the immediate threat may be less about a sudden exodus of cellphone subscribers than the gradual emergence of an alternative connectivity network backed by one of the world's most valuable technology companies.
Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile, in conjunction with the wireless trade association CTIA, are now jointly lobbying the FCC to preserve current cell-service spectrum rules, opposing proposed changes that would make it easier for satellite companies such as SpaceX to offer cellular service.
"The Commission's buildout decisions have real consequences for consumers who rely on ever-increasing wireless capacity to access the modern economy and support their day-to-day living," the trade association wrote in a letter to the FCC , filed Thursday.
The telecom incumbents' proposals for the FCC include blocking satellite providers from using 5G frequencies used to deliver wireless service and allowing wireless providers to maintain control over licensed spectrums, thereby "protect[ing] the exclusive rights of terrestrial licensees."
"CTIA commends the Commission for expanding opportunities for American consumers and businesses to benefit from next-generation terrestrial and space-based connectivity," the association wrote. articles.title_orig: Bombardier Is Making a Big $270M Push in US
articles.title_zh: Bombardier Is Making a Big $270M Push in US
articles.content_orig:
Bombardier on Friday announced it is expanding in the United State investing $270 million, including $50 million in Wichita  as part of its commitment to growing the site’s capabilities and positioning it for future growth.
The Learning Center represents one component of Bombardier’s broader investment in Wichita. Inaugurated today, the new North American Learning Center reinforces the company’s commitment to developing talent, enhancing capabilities and supporting the long-term growth of its Kansas operations. A ceremony was held on site with Kansas Governor Laura Kelly, Lieutenant Governor David Toland, Bombardier senior leaders and industry stakeholders.
The Learning Center is Bombardier’s first dedicated in-house skills development center for newly hired aircraft technicians and mechanics from across America, helping build the skilled workforce needed to support the company’s growing service and support network, enhancing long-term care and convenience for customers. The program will foster continuous learning and provide employees with a strong foundation for their careers at Bombardier.
The approximately $50 million investment brings together investments in people, infrastructure and capabilities to strengthen the Wichita site for the future. In addition to the new Learning Center, the investment includes the recently expanded Wheel and Tire Shop, which combines state-of-the-art equipment with advanced employee training to expand Bombardier’s Component Repair and Overhaul (CR&O) capabilities, enhancing quality, efficiency and safety.
“Wichita has long been an important part of Bombardier’s story, and we continue to see tremendous opportunity for the site. Our approximately $50 million investment brings together important initiatives across the site, from the new Learning Center to expanded wheel and tire capabilities, strengthening both our people and our operations. This commitment to Wichita’s future will deepen the expertise and capabilities that will allow us to deliver an even stronger experience for our customers, while position the site for continued growth” said Paul Sislian, Executive Vice President, Aircraft Sales and Bombardier Aftermarket Services.
“Since 2019, my administration has partnered with Bombardier to build up the company’s presence in Wichita, which today now includes the new Learning Center, Bombardier Group’s U.S. headquarters, home of Bombardier Defense and the employment of 1,500 Kansans,” said Governor Laura Kelly. “Bombardier’s new $50 million investment underscores the enduring strength of the partnership between Bombardier and Kansas, and one that I expect will continue long into our shared future.”
With ten service and manufacturing facilities across America, including an upcoming service center in Fort Wayne, Indiana,(1) approximately 3,500 employees and a supplier spend of $2.5 billion across America, Bombardier continues to invest in the people, infrastructure and capabilities that support its customers. Wichita remains an important part of that footprint, with recent investments positioning the site to continue evolving alongside Bombardier’s services business and the needs of its customers.

articles.title_orig: AI economic research is getting really good
articles.title_zh: AI economic research is getting really good
articles.content_orig:
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios.
Jason Furman says AI can already outperform people on much routine economic analysis, though it still falls short of the best human work in creativity. His new website illustrates how quickly the tools are changing what one researcher can produce.
AI tools can now handle work across much of the economics profession, from academic research to analysis by government agencies, consulting firms and newsroom teams. Their growing capabilities are raising questions about how people should use and supervise them.
This is reported by Axios .
“Every conversation I have with a colleague at Harvard or a think tanker in D.C. is some combination of excitement, angst and confusion,” Harvard economist Jason Furman tells Axios.
Furman, who served as the top White House economist under President Obama and now co-teaches Harvard’s introductory economics course, launched Econvitals on Friday. The site brings together economic data and analysis. Its individual features are not necessarily new, Furman notes, but producing the site took a busy professor working in his spare time, some help from research assistants and substantial assistance from Claude, with OpenAI’s Codex used for cross-checking.
Econvitals offers for free the kind of extensive number-crunching and analysis that previously could take thousands of person-hours and a seven-figure budget. One tool analyzes Federal Reserve officials’ speeches, indicating how hawkish or dovish each official is and how those views have changed over time. The site also sends email briefings on economic research and new data, and features sample economic papers generated entirely by AI from short prompts.
Furman says properly conducted AI analysis can be more factually reliable than human work, especially when fact-checking agents are used. But he says AI remains less creative than the best researchers and is better at routine analysis than at producing major new ideas. What counts as routine, he adds, shifts with each new generation of leading models.
“In terms of factual reliability, they are at this stage, if done properly, better than any human,” Furman says. “If you have fact-checking agents, what comes out is completely reliable. The hallucination idea is a combination of outdated or incompetent usage.”
“It is still not as creative and exciting as the best humans,”
“It’s really exciting how much AI can do for us and empower all of us,” he said. “Partly it’s scary. I find it is able to do a lot of what I do better than I do it, and I thought I was decently good at what I did, and that can be dispiriting at times.”
“My hope for economic research is we don’t see increase in quantity but in quality. Any idiot could write 300 papers a year now, and they’d be fine and factually correct. But I’m hoping that people don’t write more papers but write better papers,” he said.
Furman said that if he were leading the White House Council of Economic Advisers today, he would rely heavily on AI for analysis.
“If I were running the CEA today and had a choice between 20 staff members who had a combination of current Ph.D.s and future Ph.D.s versus the AI systems that we have today, I would somewhat regretfully and sadly choose the AI systems,” he said.
“You would need people at CEA to interact in meetings, to talk to the press, talk to Congress. There’s a lot of things only humans can do, but that was a fraction of what we did at CEA. For the bigger fraction of it, at this point I think machines are faster and more reliable than humans.”
For students hoping to work in research or shape economic policy, Furman’s advice is to focus on what they can contribute that is distinctive. Simply repackaging and reinterpreting data, he says, is not unique compared with other work people can do.
“I think people need to figure out how they can have value add and can do something distinctive and unique. Repackaging and reinterpreting data and numbers is not that unique and exciting compared to other things people can do.”

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.title_zh: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.content_orig:
New research, facilitated by cutting-edge techniques, led to one of the first examples of physical proof for ancient ritual animal slaughter
Animal sacrifice has played a major role in human history, from mythological stories about Odysseus to modern rituals such as Nepal’s Gadhimai Festival.
The tradition also dates back to ancient peoples we know little about. A research paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in late August suggests that the enigmatic Sanxingdui people likely practised animal sacrifice.
To reach this conclusion, researchers identified what appeared to be a sacrificial pit based on the spatial arrangement of valuable artefacts.

articles.title_orig: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.title_zh: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.content_orig:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.title_zh: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.content_orig:
How Netanyahu reshaped Israel after 18 years in power
To his supporters, he is known as “King Bibi”; but to his opponents, he is the king of security failures and corruption.
Disputes over names aside, what is not in question is that Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has left his mark on the country’s institutions, politics and social attitudes during a decades-long career that has been defined by Israel’s lurch to the right.
As he seeks re-election in Israel’s October 27 polls, analysts say his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition that he has helped create and now faces.
Born in 1949, Netanyahu entered Israel’s central political stage in the early 1990s by fuelling anger at possible peace deals with the Palestinians and Syria.
Israeli political leaders have accused him of leading incitement that motivated the 1995 assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was leading negotiations with the Palestine Liberation Organization, by an ultranationalist Israeli. Netanyahu had led rallies in which participants depicted Rabin in a Nazi SS uniform and held signs of him in the crosshairs of a gun, while others shouted “traitor”.
The Likud Party leader denies any responsibility, but former security officials have said they warned Netanyahu before the assassination and asked him to dial down his rhetoric, only for him to refuse, according to Israeli media reports.
In 1996, Netanyahu’s populist tactics succeeded at the ballot box, making him Israel’s youngest prime minister. Netanyahu’s transactional leadership style gave prominence to extreme-right and religious parties that are now an indispensable part of his right-wing alliance.
Under him, religious courts have expanded powers, including over civil and business disputes. State institutions accommodate religious agendas and allocate record levels of funding to ultra-Orthodox schools and institutions.
Netanyahu inscribed his political ideology, especially on the identity of the state and the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, into law. In 2018, the Knesset passed the so-called Nation-State Basic Law , which states – among other things – that Israel is the exclusive state of the Jewish people and also makes advancing illegal settlements a national priority.
Human rights organisations in Israel petitioned the High Court to stop the legislation from going into effect, but the petition was rejected. International experts and rights groups cite this law, among others, as evidence of Israel committing the crime of apartheid in its treatment of Palestinians.
Netanyahu also re-engineered state institutions, including Israel’s security structures, appointing loyalists and political allies to senior positions. He also clashed with security chiefs that he deemed antagonistic. And in the aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, which triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, Netanyahu deflected blame and responsibility on the security establishment, prompting Ronen Bar, who was the Shin Bet chief in 2023, to sue him for defamation.
A major change to Israeli institutions that was spearheaded by Netanyahu during his 19 on-and-off years in power affected the judiciary, which is examining lingering corruption charges that could see him serve time in prison if he is convicted. Netanyahu, who is up against three separate cases of corruption filed in 2019, denies any wrongdoing.
Under his leadership, the Knesset adopted legislation that changed the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee to ensure greater political influence for the governing coalition.
Netanyahu called it “judicial reform” to stop what he often calls a “judicial dictatorship” ruling over elected officials.
Opponents called it a “coup” that sparked wide-scale protests : a push to curtail the independence of the High Court and give politicians influence over the courts and ministerial legal advisers.
In line with his efforts to subvert independent oversight, Netanyahu tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully, to fire the attorney general.
But he succeeded in dismissing the military’s advocate general for leaking a video of Israeli soldiers gang-raping a Palestinian detainee. The soldiers were also released and cleared of charges.
At the same time, Netanyahu is dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, says his work is not over. He promises his supporters he will complete the overhaul of judicial review and press on with other highly controversial policies.
Netanyahu’s supporters and allies view him as a leader who delivers, and one who achieved what others could not. His opponents pledge to undo the damage Netanyahu caused over the past decades, pointing to corruption, social divisions and increasing international isolation as outcomes of his rule.
But undoing such formative changes, many of which are now law, may be easier said than done.

articles.title_orig: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.title_zh: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.title_zh: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title_zh: Pentagon designates China-backed campus cultural centers a threat to US national security
articles.content_orig:
Defense secretary Pete Hegseth alleges Confucius Institutes operating in disguise on US university campuses
The ⁠US defense department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses ⁠known as Confucius ⁠Institutes ​as a threat to US national security, defense secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda ⁠tools and has taken steps to ​crack down on them.
Hegseth, ‌in a ‌video posted on social media, alleged that Confucius ‌Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.
“It turns ‌out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped ​up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds ⁠of American students,” Hegseth said.
The defense department over ​the ​past two months has “systematically ​dismantled every single one of ​these organizations”, he ‌said.
The Chinese ​embassy ​in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.title_zh: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.content_orig:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman warned Friday that the United States is in a "new space race" with China, saying that the agency must recapture the urgency of the Apollo era if it hopes to return astronauts to the moon first.
China launched its first astronaut in 2003, he said, and has since built up a broad portfolio of space capabilities, including lunar missions and plans for a crewed moon landing before 2030. These rapid advances have created a competition far closer than the Cold War race that culminated in the Apollo moon landings, Isaacman said, during an Artemis update at Kennedy Space Center in Merritt Island, Florida.
"Nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass to our overseas competitors," he said. "The appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion."
NASA reaffirmed its summer plans for Artemis III, and for Artemis IV—the mission scheduled to return astronauts to the lunar surface—in 2028. The agency will continue to depend on Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to achieve these goals.
According to NASA officials, Artemis III will be a two-week mission involving four astronauts and a series of docking demonstrations in Earth's orbit, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing the lunar landers. The mission will not travel to the moon but is designed to test systems and operations needed for future lunar landings.
Artemis III will require multiple launches in quick succession from Florida and give crews an opportunity to conduct docking exercises with both commercial spacecraft, NASA leaders said.
During the briefing, Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons praised SpaceX's rapid development pace.
"We're seeing lots of hardware, lots of quick changes, and an absolute blistering pace of production," he said.
The agency's push comes as China works toward its publicly stated goal of landing astronauts on the moon before 2030, raising concerns among U.S. officials that America could lose momentum in a domain it once dominated.
Isaacman repeatedly invoked the Apollo era, arguing that NASA should draw lessons from when the agency progressed from Apollo 7's first crewed mission to Apollo 11's lunar landing within nine months.
"It's a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months," he said.
While emphasizing that NASA will not compromise safety, Isaacman said the agency is working to cut bureaucracy, speed decision-making and increase the pace of hardware development.
The broader goal, he said, extends beyond simply returning astronauts to the moon.
"This will not be a repeat of flags and footprints," Isaacman said.
He described future lunar missions as laying the groundwork for a permanent human presence beyond Earth.
"These vehicles are being designed to dramatically reduce the cost of delivering mass to orbit and to the moon, to support longer surface operations, enable more frequent astronaut missions, and transform what will begin as a small scientific outpost into something that may one day resemble a city on the lunar surface, " Isaacman said.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.title_zh: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.content_orig:
China’s remote access alone is expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year
China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research.
Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP).
While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.
